title: How jet engines work
hook: A jet engine has nothing solid to push against: it just throws air out of its back. So how does that hurl a jumbo jet down a runway fast enough to fly?
oneBreath: A jet engine works by throwing air backwards: push air back hard and the air pushes the engine forwards. To throw it hard, the engine squeezes the air, burns fuel in it so it expands and rushes out of the back, and uses some of that rush to spin the turbine that drives the squeezing. Airliner engines add a huge fan that moves lots of extra air, which saves fuel.

ideas.title: Throw something back, get pushed forward
ideas.oneLine: Push something backwards and it pushes you forwards just as hard, so an engine needs nothing solid behind it to push on.

ideas.title: Thrust: air per second times speed added
ideas.oneLine: How hard an engine pushes depends on how much air it throws back each second and how much faster it makes that air go.

ideas.title: Suck, squeeze, bang, blow
ideas.oneLine: Follow the air through the engine: in at the front, squeezed by the compressor, burned with fuel, then blasted out of the nozzle.

ideas.title: Why squeeze the air before burning it
ideas.oneLine: Squeezing the air before heating it lets the engine turn more of the fuel's energy into a faster jet.

ideas.title: The turbine pays for the squeeze
ideas.oneLine: Some of the hot gas's energy spins a turbine, which turns the shaft that drives the compressor at the front.

ideas.title: Big fans: more air, less fuel
ideas.oneLine: Airliner engines use a huge fan to push lots of extra air a little faster, giving the same thrust for less fuel.

calibration.q: In space there is no air at all. Could a rocket engine, which works like a jet, still push a spacecraft forwards there?
options: No: with no air behind it, there is nothing to push against
Yes: it pushes on the gas it throws out
Only weakly, by pushing on the thin dust of space
calibration.why: Yes. The engine pushes its gas out backwards, and the gas pushes the engine forwards just as hard, so nothing behind the spacecraft is needed. Air was never what the engine pushed against.

calibration.q: Why does a jet engine burn fuel?
options: To heat the air so it expands and rushes out faster
Because the flame itself pushes on the back of the engine
To keep the engine warm in the cold air at height
calibration.why: Burning fuel heats the squeezed air, so it expands and rushes out much faster than it came in. Faster air thrown back means a bigger push; the flame does not push on anything.
